flawed_step: The key step would be: "take a vertex v of degree at least 2; some neighbor of v must be a leaf." Nothing justifies this. A neighbor of v can have its own neighbors besides v, and once n >= 5 there is room for every neighbor of v to have degree at least 2.
counterexample: The path P5 with edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-5 (n = 5). Vertex 3 has degree 2. Its only neighbors are 2 and 4, and each of those has degree 2, so neither is a leaf.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. I tried to show that any vertex of degree at least 2 has a leaf as a neighbor, but that step fails. In the path on 5 vertices (1-2-3-4-5), the middle vertex 3 has degree 2, and both of its neighbors (2 and 4) also have degree 2, so it touches no leaf. The same kind of example works for n = 6 and n = 7, for instance the paths P6 and P7. The claim does hold when n is 4 or less.
